Morgan le Fay. In Arthurian legend, also known as Morgana or Morgen, a powerful enchantress and magical figure whose relationship to King Arthur is ambiguous and shifts across versions. Sometimes she is presented as his sister, sometimes as his romantic interest or teacher, and sometimes as his antagonist. Her mastery of magic, residence in the mystical realm of Avalon, and complex motivations make her one of the most enigmatic figures in Arthurian literature.

Morgan's parentage and relationship to Arthur vary across sources. In some versions, she is the half-sister of Arthur, daughter of Igraine and the Duke of Cornwall or Uther Pendragon. In others, she is merely a powerful magical woman with no blood relation. She is typically depicted as a master of magic and healing. She studies with Merlin in some accounts and becomes his rival or successor as a wielder of supernatural power. Morgan dwells in Avalon, the mystical island realm hidden from the mortal world. She is often portrayed as one of the three queens, or magical women, who rule this otherworldly space and possess knowledge of healing, prophecy, and transformation.

Her relationship with Arthur encompasses contradictory roles. She is protective sister, romantic rival, antagonist seeking to undermine his rule, and ultimately the figure who ferries his dying body to Avalon for healing and potential resurrection. In some versions, notably Tennyson's poetry, Morgan is Arthur's daughter by Guinevere or another woman, and her hatred for Arthur stems from his refusal to acknowledge her. In others, she is his devoted protector. Morgan is sometimes a romantic interest to Lancelot or other knights. Her magical powers and independence from conventional morality make her alluring and dangerous to the male-centered Arthurian society. Over time, particularly in medieval literature, Morgan has been portrayed both sympathetically as a complex woman navigating patriarchal constraints through magic and will, and negatively as a seductress and betrayer. Modern interpretations often reclaim her as a figure of feminine power, representing an alternative to the masculine heroism that dominates Arthurian legend.
